cases.title: Leading Together Under Pressure
cases.lede: Team coaching with senior leadership to support alignment.
challenge: High pressure and fatigue
Strained dynamics
Unspoken impact
A need for shared identity
shifted: Greater clarity and alignment around roles, decision-making, and leadership expectations.
Improved communication and trust, including more direct feedback and fewer workarounds.
Increased self-awareness and empathy, as leaders better understood how stress and protection strategies were shaping their interactions.
A renewed sense of shared purpose and leadership identity, grounded in values rather than reactivity.
cases.takeaway: Under sustained pressure and grief, a senior team rebuilt trust by naming what they’d been carrying and articulating how they wanted to lead together.
quotes: Jenna and Stacy are phenomenal coaches who help you and your team to discover your strengths and perform at your highest level. They are extremely perceptive, identifying issues easily and providing tailored and actionable advice to help you and your team get to the next level. They both bring an uplifting and authentic approach to their coaching, which makes any session with them fly by! — Leadership Team Member

Jenna and Stacy meshed well with our team and were able to bring the right energy to help us work through our more difficult issues. I particularly appreciated both Jenna and Stacy’s calling out when we need to grapple with something a bit more, explaining/synthesizing things for the group, and being particularly flexible on timing and the agenda. — Leadership Team Member

cases.title: Developing Endurance and Agency
cases.lede: 1:1 coaching with a senior leader to navigate relational tension.
challenge: A power dynamic where honest upward feedback felt risky.
Recurring interpersonal tension that drained energy and focus.
A growing sense of burnout and disillusionment with how the work was being done.
An unspoken question: Is the stress we’re carrying actually necessary?
shifted: Greater self-trust and emotional regulation in high-stakes interactions.
Increased clarity about what was theirs to hold—and what was not.
More direct, grounded conversations with the Executive Director.
The courage to name patterns affecting morale and sustainability.
A renewed sense of alignment with the mission, rooted in how the work could be done, not just what the work achieved.
cases.takeaway: Coaching didn’t fix the organization—it moved one leader from enduring stress to actively shaping healthier conditions, with clarity, courage, and agency.

cases.title: Building Conditions for Results
cases.lede: Retreats to invest in team effectiveness from the jump.
challenge: New team members were hired to step into new roles while still learning one another’s strengths, preferences, and needs.
Expectations around roles, workflows, and decision-making had not yet been fully articulated - it was only the second week on the job for 2 members of the team.
The team needed to translate Empower’s broader mission into a clear, shared vision for development work in the year ahead.
There was a strong desire to build trust and sustainability early, rather than retrofitting norms after challenges emerged.
approach: Anchoring to Mission and Leadership Expectations
shifted: A shared understanding that team effectiveness is a strategic lever. One team member wrote, “I walked out of the session feeling impressed about my new organization’s investment in team effectiveness and positive team dynamics.”
Clear alignment between Empower’s organizational mission and strategy and the Development team’s own vision, priorities, and ways of working.

Increased trust and relational depth, allowing team members to collaborate more openly, surface challenges earlier, and rely on one another with confidence. One team member reflected that, ” Understanding each other’s strengths, motivations, and blind spots is going to be so much easier now, which will unlock our ability to collaborate with understanding, patience, and pride in our teammates and ourselves.”

Defined roles, decision-making authority, and interdependencies that reduce friction and support efficient, coordinated execution. A team member wrote, in reflection, “Had we not done this retreat, we might have been in danger of failing to see how each of us can fit into and contribute to our team’s goals.”
Explicitly stated team habits and routines around communication, feedback, meetings, and workload management.
cases.takeaway: Building trust and shared norms at a team’s formation—before problems emerge—set the conditions for results, instead of retrofitting culture after strain sets in.
quotes: I walked out of the session feeling impressed about my new organization’s investment in team effectiveness and positive team dynamics. Understanding each other’s strengths, motivations, and blind spots is going to be so much easier now, which will unlock our ability to collaborate with understanding, patience, and pride in our teammates and ourselves. Had we not done this retreat, we might have been in danger of failing to see how each of us can fit into and contribute to our team’s goals. — Client

I walked out of the session feeling confident about my team’s roles and responsibilities and how we are aligned on achieving our overall mission. Getting to know each other and how we operate at our best is going to be so much easier now, which will unlock our ability to accomplish our objectives and realize our strategy for the year and beyond. — Client

cases.title: Repairing a Ruptured Relationship
cases.lede: 2:2 coaching to repair a manager-employee relationship.
challenge: Expectations felt unclear and misaligned, leading to frustration on both sides.
Feedback was experienced as unproductive and, at times, threatening rather than developmental.
Each person questioned the other’s intentions, assuming criticism or dismissal where none was intended.
Anxiety and risk‑mitigation replaced trust, openness, and shared problem‑solving.
shifted: Increased clarity around expectations, priorities, and communication norms.
Reduced fear and defensiveness, replaced by greater curiosity and generosity of interpretation.
More consistent, predictable feedback routines and norms to support earlier communication when challenges arose.
cases.takeaway: 2x2 coaching turned a cycle of defensiveness and mistrust between a manager and their report into clearer expectations, safer feedback, and restored good faith.

cases.title: Choosing the Culture We Build on Campaigns
cases.lede: Team and leadership development in a statewide coordinated political campaign.
challenge: Middle managers were carrying significant emotional and operational load.
Team culture was being shaped in real time, often under extreme pressure.
The team wanted space to reflect, connect, and build resilience. Timing and system-level constraints complicated the waters.
There was a real risk that insight would not translate into sustained behavior change without intentional follow-through.
shifted: Stronger relationships and a deeper sense of alignment across the team.
Increased awareness of how personal stress affects team culture.
Renewed commitment to centering joy, assuming positive intent, and supporting one another more intentionally.
Greater clarity about individual growth edges as managers and leaders.
Virtual sessions were less effective given campaign timing and unaddressed system-level pressures.
Leaders wanted more role-specific spaces (e.g., ROD-only).
cases.takeaway: Even under relentless campaign pressure, leaders found that culture is a choice—and that time to reconnect as people, not just roles, is what makes it hold.
quotes: I learned how much my stress impacts team culture, and that I have real choices about how I show up every day. Campaign Leader
This created space to connect as people, not just as roles. It reminded me that we choose the culture we build, even under pressure. Regional Leader
I’m committed to centering joy, assuming positive intent, and being more thoughtful about how I communicate, especially when things are hard.
I realized I need to delegate more, ask for what I need, and seek counsel from my peers instead of carrying everything alone.
The team cares deeply about each other and this work. Being together in person helped that come back into focus.

I walked out of the session feeling impressed about my new organization’s investment in team effectiveness and positive team dynamics. Understanding each other’s strengths, motivations, and blind spots is going to be so much easier now, which will unlock our ability to collaborate with understanding, patience, and pride in our teammates and ourselves. Had we not done this retreat, we might have been in danger of failing to see how each of us can fit into and contribute to our team’s goals.

resources.title: Values & Energy
paras: Clarity on your values and energy is the foundation for leading from a grounded place. This worksheet helps you name what matters most and what sustains you. Then you can make choices that align with both.
Naming your values, first and foremost for yourself, changes what you'll let go of and what you'll fight for.
This list isn't exhaustive. If a value that matters to you is missing, add it.
Consider the parts of work that energize you and what quietly depletes you. Think across the full space of your career to answer the following.
heads: The single thing I want to remember from this is…

resources.title: After Action Review
paras: Use this after you finish a project or a specific phase of work. The goal is to build collective understanding about what happened, learn from it together, and apply that learning to the work ahead.
heads: What did we set out to do, together?
What were the gaps, and why did they happen?

paras: Each person fills this out for their own role. Then share it with your team, so everyone can see what you own, how you work, and where you need each other.

resources.title: Thinking About a Team Retreat?
paras: Team retreat planning checklist
A starting place for leaders and teams in the early stages of deciding why, how, and when to gather your people.
You have a feeling your team needs time together, away from the day to day. Maybe you don't have a date, a venue, or a clear reason yet. That's a fine place to start.

This checklist helps you get your thinking in order before you commit to anything. It covers the decisions most teams face, in the order they usually come up, along with the questions worth talking through with the people who will plan with you.
heads: Get Clear on Why You're Gathering
Decide Who Plans and Who Leads the Room
Sketch the Shape of the Day

resources.title: Your career, in chapters.
paras: Load saved work Save my work Print or Save as PDF Step 1 of 8 Career Reflection Your career, in chapters. Take an hour with this. Move slowly. The goal is to notice the throughlines, the turns, and the parts of the story you haven't told in a while.
Sometimes, reflecting on your career can come into focus when you can name the eras. Don't worry about being neat; you can come back and rearrange. Add as many as you need.
Name the decisions that have shaped your path and your learning.
For each era you named, rate how alive, motivated, in flow you felt. Then notice the shape of the line.
heads: If I had to name the single thread that runs through everything I've done — the thing I keep coming back to — it would be…
